# 王法正理論

**Category:** 瑜伽部類
**Original Category:** 瑜伽部
**Byline:** 彌勒菩薩造  唐 玄奘譯
**Dynasty:** 唐
**Date:** 649
**Juans:** 1

- 玄奘 (A000294)

## Summary (Ask Bunkankun 聞分館君)

A single-fascicle treatise on the *dhárma* of kingship, attributed in Chinese tradition to **Maitreya** ([彌勒菩薩](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E5%BD%8C%E5%8B%92%E8%8F%A9%E8%96%A9)) and translated by [玄奘](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%84%E5%A5%98) in the Táng. Preserved in the *Taishō* at T31n1615; sub-section of the great Yogācāra-doctrinal *Yújiā shīdì lùn* 瑜伽師地論 (the *Yogācārabhūmi*) tradition. The text is one of the principal Indian Buddhist *rājadharma* texts to enter the Chinese canon, and the only one preserved with a Maitreya-attribution.

**Abstract**

The *Wángfǎ zhènglǐ lùn* is a Yogācāra extract: in the Sanskrit tradition the same material survives embedded in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* section of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. The Chinese transmission as a stand-alone text is the result of [玄奘](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%84%E5%A5%98)'s practice of translating doctrinally significant sub-sections of the *Yújiā* as independent treatises — a pattern also seen with the [KR6n0112](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6n/KR6n0112) *Guān suǒyuányuán lùn*, the [KR6n0119](https://ask.bunkankun.org/KR6/KR6n/KR6n0119) *Zhǎngzhōng lùn*, and others.

The dating is precise: [玄奘](https://ask.bunkankun.org/Persons/%E7%8E%84%E5%A5%98)'s translation activity on the Yogācāra corpus occurred at Cí'ēnsì in Chángān between his return from India (645) and his death (664); the closely-related *Yújiā shīdì lùn* was completed in Zhēnguān 22 (648), so the *Wángfǎ zhènglǐ lùn* is most likely from the immediate translation cycle that followed, conventionally dated **Zhēnguān 23 = 649**.

The text is doctrinally important as the principal Mahāyāna Buddhist statement of *rāja-dharma* in the Chinese canon. Its nine vices include lack of self-mastery, violence, anger, niggardliness, accepting flattery, thoughtless action, neglect of the good *dharma*, ingratitude, and self-indulgence; the corresponding nine virtues are their opposites. The work was widely cited in late-Táng and Sòng Buddhist literature as the canonical Buddhist statement on royal duty.
